kurals.tamil:
வான்நின்று உலகம் வழங்கி வருதலால்
தான்அமிழ்தம் என்றுணரற் பாற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaan nindru ulagam vazhangi varudhalaal,
Thaan amizhdham endru unarar paatru.
kurals.meaning: Because the world keeps going and living only through rain that falls without fail, rain itself deserves to be recognised as amrita — the nectar that sustains undying life.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a plant on your windowsill. Water it, and it stays green and grows; forget it for a week, and it droops and dies. This kural says the whole world is that plant, and rain is the water. Because rain keeps everything alive, we should treat it like the most precious drink there is.
kurals.university: Valluvar's second chapter makes a striking structural choice: immediately after invoking God he turns not to ritual or scripture but to வான் (vaan), the sky and the rain that comes from it. The key term is அமிழ்தம் (amizhdham), the Tamil form of Sanskrit अमृत (amṛta), the deathless nectar of the gods — so rain is not merely useful but the very substance of continued life, which is why G. U. Pope rendered it "the true ambrosial food of all that lives." The verb வழங்கி (vazhangi, "conducting itself, carrying on") frames the world as an ongoing transaction that rain alone keeps in motion. Medieval commentators such as Parimelazhagar read the chapter as establishing the material precondition of அறம் (aram, virtue) itself, and modern secular and ecological readers have seized on exactly this move: Valluvar grounds ethics in a physical dependency rather than in divine command.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "Amrit is in the Waters, in the Waters there is healing balm"
hinduism.explanation: In this Vedic hymn to the Waters, the poet declares that the immortal nectar (amṛta) and every medicine that heals are literally present within water itself.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the same identification Valluvar makes — rain is not merely like nectar, it is amrita.
hinduism._accuracy_note: An almost word-for-word conceptual match: the Sanskrit amṛta and the Tamil amizhdham are the same word, both predicated of water.

christianity.quote_or_event: "Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness."
christianity.explanation: Paul, preaching at Lystra, argues that rain and the harvest it produces are themselves sufficient evidence of a good God at work in the world.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats rain as the single most visible thing that keeps human life going and worth honouring.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on rain as life-sustaining gift; adds a theological claim about God's witness that the Kural deliberately avoids.

islam.quote_or_event: "And We have sent down blessed rain from the sky and made grow thereby gardens and grain from the harvest"
islam.explanation: The Qur'an calls rain mubārakan — "blessed" — and names it as the direct cause of every garden and grain crop.
islam.tie_back: The epithet "blessed" for rain parallels the Kural's "amrita": rain is singled out as the uniquely life-giving substance.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on rain-as-blessing-and-sustainer; the Kural's specific nectar-of-immortality figure has no exact Qur'anic counterpart.

judaism.quote_or_event: "Rabbi Abbahu said: The day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead."
judaism.explanation: The Talmud's praise of rainfall ranks it above resurrection, reasoning that resurrection benefits only the righteous while rain benefits righteous and wicked alike.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts rank rain alongside immortality itself — the Kural calls it nectar, the Talmud calls it greater than the raising of the dead.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 7a (Koren–Steinsaltz, William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Unusually close: both traditions independently place rain in the same conceptual register as deathlessness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Even as the great cloud, Kâsyapa, after expanding over the whole universe, pours out the same water and recreates by it all grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees"
buddhism.explanation: In the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, one cloud rains impartially on the whole world and every plant, small or large, takes what it can and grows — the image for how one Dharma nourishes all beings.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's premise that a single rain is what recreates and sustains every living thing in the world.
buddhism.source: Saddharma-Pundarika (Lotus Sutra), Chapter 5, "On Plants" (Kern translation, SBE vol. 21)
buddhism._accuracy_note: The literal rain imagery matches well, but in the sutra rain is chiefly a simile for the Dharma rather than the physical subject.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Homer, the gods live on ambrosia and nectar, the food and drink that make them deathless; Calypso sets ambrosia before Hermes, and gods use it to preserve mortal bodies from decay.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ambrosia is Greek myth's substance of immortality, reserved for the Olympians and occasionally used to keep a human body incorruptible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek ambrosia and the Kural's amizhdham descend from the same Indo-European root (*n̥-mr̥tos, "undying"), so Valluvar is quite literally calling rain the ambrosia of the world.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 5.92–94, 199 (ambrosia and nectar of the gods)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The etymological and conceptual kinship is real and illuminating, but Homer never connects ambrosia to rainfall — the link is comparative, not thematic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "Thales, the founder of this school of philosophy, says the principle is water … getting the notion perhaps from seeing that the nutriment of all things is moist, and that heat itself is generated from the moist and kept alive by it"
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle reports the first recorded Greek philosophical thesis: water is the archē, the first principle out of which everything comes and by which everything is nourished.
philosophy.tie_back: Both Thales and Valluvar reach for water as the one substance without which the world cannot be or continue.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on water as universal sustainer; Thales makes a cosmological claim about origin, while the Kural makes a practical claim about ongoing maintenance.

kurals.tamil:
துப்பார்க்குத் துப்பாய துப்பாக்கித் துப்பார்க்குத்
துப்பாய தூஉம் மழை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thuppaarkkuth thuppaaya thuppaakkith thuppaarkkuth,
Thuppaaya thooum mazhai.
kurals.meaning: Rain produces the food that those who eat will eat, and then, for those same eaters, rain becomes the drink they drink; it is both the maker of food and food itself.
kurals.elementary: Rain is like a cook who grows the vegetables, cooks the meal, and then also pours you a glass of water to go with it. It does both jobs at once — it makes your food, and it is your drink.
kurals.university: This is one of the most technically dazzling couplets in the Kural: the syllable துப்பு (thuppu) is repeated five times, shifting sense each time between "food/sustenance," "strength," and the verbal sense "to eat or enjoy," a figure Tamil poetics calls யமகம் (yamakam). The elongated தூஉம் (thooum) is an அளபெடை, a metrical lengthening that also lets the word carry the sense of drinking. Semantically the verse makes a double claim that anticipates modern hydrology and nutrition alike — rain is the upstream cause of food and is simultaneously the substance consumed — a point later elaborated in chapter 104 on உழவு (agriculture). Commentators from Parimelazhagar to Salomon Pappaiah note that this two-sidedness is precisely why rain, and not the farmer, is given primacy in the book's opening argument.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "All living bodies subsist on food grains, which are produced from rain. Rains are produced by performance of yajña [sacrifice], and yajña is born of prescribed duties."
hinduism.explanation: Krishna sets out a causal chain — action produces sacrifice, sacrifice produces rain, rain produces grain, grain produces living beings.
hinduism.tie_back: The first two links of that chain are exactly this Kural: rain makes the food that eaters eat.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on rain as the producer of food for all who eat; the Gita adds a ritual cause above rain that the Kural omits.

christianity.quote_or_event: "For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:"
christianity.explanation: Isaiah uses rainfall as a figure for the reliability of God's word, but the image itself is a precise account of rain producing seed and bread.
christianity.tie_back: "Bread to the eater" is almost a translation of துப்பார்க்குத் துப்பாய — food for those who eat.
christianity._accuracy_note: Exceptionally close on rain-makes-food-for-eaters; the verse does not add the Kural's second claim that rain is itself the drink.

islam.quote_or_event: "It is He who sends down rain from the sky; from it is drink and from it is foliage in which you pasture [animals]."
islam.explanation: The verse divides rain's benefit in two: it is the water people drink, and it is the growth that feeds their livestock.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact double structure — rain as the drink and rain as the maker of food.
islam._accuracy_note: The strongest match in the chapter: both texts explicitly name rain as simultaneously the drink and the source of food.

judaism.quote_or_event: "He watereth the hills from his chambers: the earth is satisfied with the fruit of thy works. He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth;"
judaism.explanation: Psalm 104's creation hymn traces a direct line from rain falling on the hills to grass for cattle and bread for human beings.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural it treats rain as the single upstream cause of everything eaters eat.
judaism._accuracy_note: Solid on rain-produces-food; a general Tanakh psalm rather than a distinctively rabbinic source, and it lacks the rain-as-drink half.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "What is one? All beings subsist on food."
buddhism.explanation: The very first question put to a Buddhist novice, and its answer — the most basic fact about existence is that every living thing depends on nutriment (āhāra).
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's premise that eating is the universal condition of life, though it stops short of naming rain as its source.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Genuine on universal dependence on food, but the Pali canon is silent here about rain, so the rain half of the Kural is missing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demeter, goddess of grain, gives the young prince Triptolemus of Eleusis the first seed corn and sends him out in a winged chariot to teach agriculture to all mankind, so that human beings can eat cultivated food rather than forage.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Eleusinian myth makes grain a divine gift rather than a human invention, and makes the goddess of that gift the centre of Greece's most important mystery cult.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the origin of the food that eaters eat outside human labour, in a power that must give before people can consume.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter (and the Eleusinian Triptolemus tradition)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A real parallel on food as gift rather than achievement, but Greek myth assigns that role to grain and the goddess, not to rain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "Now the first and greatest of necessities is food, which is the condition of life and existence."
philosophy.explanation: Socrates, building an imaginary city from scratch, ranks food ahead of every other need as the precondition of a society existing at all.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the philosophical premise the Kural is arguing from — that everything else in human life is downstream of what people eat.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the priority-of-food claim exactly; Plato is silent on rain, so only half of the Kural's two-step argument is present.

kurals.tamil:
விண்இன்று பொய்ப்பின் விரிநீர் வியனுலகத்து
உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி.
kurals.transliteration:
Vin indru poyppin virineer viyanulagaththu,
Ul nindru udatrum pasi.
kurals.meaning: If the sky breaks its promise and no rain comes, then hunger will take up residence inside this wide, sea-encircled world and torment every life in it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine standing right next to a swimming pool while you are terribly thirsty — all that water, and not a drop you can drink. This kural says the world is surrounded by ocean, but if rain stops falling, people will still go hungry, and hunger will hurt from the inside.
kurals.university: The verb பொய்ப்பின் (poyppin) literally means "if it lies" — Valluvar personifies the sky as a party that can break faith, which is why English renderings often speak of clouds that "deceive." The phrase விரிநீர் வியனுலகம் (virineer viyanulagam), "the broad world of spreading waters," sets up a deliberate irony: a planet ringed by ocean can still starve, because salt sea is not rain. உடற்றும் (udatrum) is a strong verb of tormenting or harrying, and உள்நின்று (ul nindru, "standing within") places the affliction inside the body rather than outside it. The couplet is frequently cited in modern Tamil discussion of drought and food security precisely because it distinguishes water-in-general from usable fresh water.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rāmāyaṇa, the kingdom of Anga under King Romapada suffers a devastating drought and famine; on the advice of his counsellors the king brings the young ascetic Rishyasringa into the land, and with his arrival the rains return and the famine ends.
hinduism.explanation: The episode treats a failed monsoon as a national emergency whose remedy is sought through a holy person, and it opens the Rāmāyaṇa's account of Dasharatha's sacrifice.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that when the sky fails, hunger becomes the defining condition of an entire kingdom.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A genuine drought-and-famine narrative, but the emphasis falls on the ritual remedy rather than on hunger itself as the Kural has it.

christianity.quote_or_event: "And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word."
christianity.explanation: Elijah announces a multi-year drought as judgement on Ahab; the narrative that follows describes a severe famine gripping Samaria until the rains return.
christianity.tie_back: It is the same sequence the Kural compresses into two lines: the sky withholds, and hunger takes hold of the land.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match on no-rain-then-famine; framed as divine judgement, which the Kural does not invoke.

islam.quote_or_event: "Say, 'Have you considered: if your water was to become sunken [into the earth], then who could bring you flowing water?'"
islam.explanation: The Qur'an closes Surah al-Mulk with a challenge: human beings have no fallback if the water that sustains them simply disappears.
islam.tie_back: Both verses press the reader to imagine the world's water failing and to recognise that nothing human can substitute for it.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the thought-experiment of water failing; speaks of groundwater vanishing rather than naming hunger as the consequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: "And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest … So two or three cities wandered unto one city, to drink water; but they were not satisfied: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD."
judaism.explanation: Amos describes a partial drought — rain on one town, none on the next — and the desperate migration of thirsty, hungry populations that followed.
judaism.tie_back: It gives concrete social texture to the Kural's abstract claim that a failed sky means hunger settling into a whole land.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on rain withheld producing region-wide want; a prophetic Tanakh text rather than a distinctively rabbinic one.

buddhism.quote_or_event: According to the Pali commentarial tradition, the city of Vesālī was struck by drought, which brought famine, then corpses in the streets, then plague; the Buddha was invited, walked the city reciting the Ratana Sutta, and a great rain fell that washed the city clean and ended the crisis.
buddhism.explanation: The story is the traditional origin narrative for one of Theravada Buddhism's most widely chanted protective discourses.
buddhism.tie_back: Its causal order is the Kural's own: rain fails first, and hunger and suffering follow from that failure.
buddhism.source: Ratana Sutta (Sn 2.1 / Khp 6) and its commentarial background narrative on the famine at Vesālī
buddhism._accuracy_note: The famine-from-drought link is explicit, but it comes from commentary rather than canonical text, and the focus is on the protective chant.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "Often even a whole city suffers for a bad man who sins and devises presumptuous deeds, and the son of Cronos lays great trouble upon the people, famine and plague together, so that the men perish away, and their women do not bear children, and their houses become few"
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that Zeus punishes collective injustice with collective calamity, and famine heads his list of instruments.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural's picture of hunger afflicting an entire population from within, though Hesiod traces the cause to human wrongdoing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on society-wide famine; Hesiod's moral causation is an addition the Kural's plainly meteorological statement does not make.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "Famine seems to be the last, the most dreadful resource of nature."
philosophy.explanation: Malthus argues that when milder checks on population fail, hunger is the ultimate and most terrible constraint that reasserts the limits of the earth's productivity.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat hunger as the inescapable consequence when the land's capacity to produce food gives out.
philosophy.source: Thomas Robert Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), Chapter VII
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very strong on famine as nature's final constraint; Malthus's driver is population growth rather than a failed monsoon.

kurals.tamil:
ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர் புயல்என்னும்
வாரி வளங்குன்றிக் கால்.
kurals.transliteration:
Erin uzhaaar uzhavar puyal ennum,
Vaari valam kundrik kaal.
kurals.meaning: When rain — that great revenue-stream — falls short in its yield, even the farmers will stop driving the plough.
kurals.elementary: A bicycle is useless if the tyres have no air in them; you can own it, but you cannot ride it. This kural says a farmer's plough is like that. However strong the farmer is, if the rain does not come, the plough just sits there.
kurals.university: The economic vocabulary here is deliberate: வாரி (vaari) is a revenue term, the yield or income of a realm, so Valluvar literally calls rain the kingdom's principal income stream — a framing that anticipates the Poruṭpāl's treatment of statecraft and chapter 104 on உழவு (agriculture). உழாஅர் (uzhaaar, "they do not plough") carries an அளபெடை, a metrical elongation that lends the line a note of weary finality. புயல் (puyal) denotes rain in its abundant, gusting monsoon form rather than a drizzle. The couplet's force lies in its choice of the farmer as subject: of all people the ploughman is the most industrious, and if even he downs tools, no amount of human effort can substitute for the sky.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya's Arthaśāstra instructs the state's superintendent of agriculture to measure annual rainfall in droṇas for each type of terrain — dry, wet and marshy country — and to decide which crops may be sown on the basis of how much rain has actually fallen.
hinduism.explanation: The treatise makes rainfall data an explicit input to agricultural planning and revenue forecasting for the realm.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the administrative version of this Kural: below a certain rainfall the ploughing simply does not happen.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book II, Chapter 24 (Shamasastry translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A genuine classical Indian text linking rainfall directly to whether and what farmers sow; paraphrased rather than quoted because translations of the measurement passage vary.

christianity.quote_or_event: "Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain."
christianity.explanation: James takes the farmer as the model of patience precisely because the farmer's work is hostage to rain he cannot command.
christianity.tie_back: Both verses make the farmer's dependence on rainfall the definitive example of human effort waiting on the sky.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very strong on the farmer-waits-for-rain motif; James uses it as a moral simile for patience, the Kural as a statement of fact.

islam.quote_or_event: "And have you seen that [seed] which you sow? Is it you who makes it grow, or are We the grower?"
islam.explanation: The Qur'an confronts the farmer with the limits of his own agency: he can sow, but the growth is not in his hands.
islam.tie_back: It makes the Kural's point from the other direction — ploughing and sowing are worthless unless a power beyond the farmer supplies the water.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the farmer's dependence; frames the dependence theologically rather than naming rainfall shortfall as the Kural does.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah prescribes an escalating public response when the winter rains fail: after successive rounds of communal fasts pass unanswered, Jews are to cut back on business, on building and planting, on betrothals and weddings, and on greetings between neighbours.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law treats a failed rainy season as grounds for suspending ordinary economic activity, including planting itself.
judaism.tie_back: It legislates exactly what the Kural observes — when the rain does not come, the planting stops.
judaism._accuracy_note: A real halakhic link between failed rain and suspended planting; the Mishnah's framework is liturgical and penitential, not agronomic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Conviction is my seed, / austerity my rain, / discernment my yoke & plow, / conscience my pole, / mind my yoke-tie, / mindfulness my plowshare & goad."
buddhism.explanation: Challenged by the brahmin farmer Kasi Bharadvaja to justify eating without ploughing, the Buddha answers by mapping each part of the plough team onto a quality of spiritual practice.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha's metaphor concedes the Kural's literal premise — no rain, no ploughing — which is exactly why rain can stand for the indispensable element in any cultivation.
buddhism.source: Kasi Bhāradvāja Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.4 (Thanissaro Bhikkhu translation)
buddhism._accuracy_note: A verified canonical text that pairs rain with ploughing, but it works as spiritual allegory rather than a claim about agriculture.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "Mark, when you hear the voice of the crane who cries year by year from the clouds above, for she gives the signal for ploughing and shows the season of rainy winter; but she vexes the heart of the man who has no oxen."
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farming calendar ties the start of ploughing to the arrival of the rainy season, announced by migrating cranes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both poets treat ploughing as an activity that begins only when the rains arrive and is meaningless without them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on rain as the trigger for ploughing; Hesiod describes timing rather than the failure case the Kural addresses.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "A prayer of the Athenians: Rain, rain, O dear Zeus, down on the ploughed fields of the Athenians and on the plains."
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius cites this old Athenian prayer as his model of how one should pray at all — simply, nobly, and for the one thing the fields actually need.
philosophy.tie_back: It puts the Kural's insight in the mouth of a whole city: the ploughed field is finished work until rain falls on it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Explicitly joins rain and ploughed fields; it is a prayer rather than the Kural's flat causal statement, and wording varies slightly across translations.

kurals.tamil:
கெடுப்பதூஉம் கெட்டார்க்குச் சார்வாய்மற் றாங்கே
எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை.
kurals.transliteration:
Keduppadhoum kettaarkkuch chaarvaai matraange,
Eduppadhoum ellaam mazhai.
kurals.meaning: Rain is what ruins people, and rain is also what comes alongside the ruined and raises them up again — it does both, and it does all of it.
kurals.elementary: Fire can burn your hand, and fire can also cook your dinner — the same thing can hurt you or help you. This kural says rain is like that: too little or too much can wreck everything, and then the right rain at the right time puts it all back together.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a tight antithesis — கெடுப்பது ("that which destroys") against எடுப்பது ("that which lifts up") — each carrying the அளபெடை elongation -தூஉம் that gives the line its rocking, pendulum rhythm. Commentators divide on the mechanism of ruin: Parimelazhagar reads கெடுப்பது as rain destroying by withholding itself, while modern paraphrasts such as Kalaignar Karunanidhi allow the destructive flood as well, and both readings are defensible from the Tamil. Strikingly, Valluvar assigns the double agency to rain itself rather than to a god who sends it, and the closing எல்லாம் ("all of it") refuses to split the credit. The verse is a favourite of Tamil ecological writing because it treats the same natural force as both hazard and remedy without moralising either face.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "O Arjuna, I control heat, the rain and the drought. I am immortality, and I am also death personified. Both being and nonbeing are in Me."
hinduism.explanation: Krishna claims both the withholding and the sending of rain as his own act, and in the same breath claims both deathlessness and death.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's double agency exactly — the identical power that destroys by withholding also restores by pouring.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 9.19 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Outstanding match: withholding and sending rain, ruin and restoration, are held together in one statement just as in the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: "He causeth it to come, whether for correction, or for his land, or for mercy."
christianity.explanation: Elihu, describing the clouds, says the same rain may arrive as chastisement, as ordinary provision for the land, or as sheer mercy.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim that rain both ruins and raises, condensed into a single verse.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on rain's twofold effect; Job attributes the choice to God, where the Kural leaves the agency with rain itself.

islam.quote_or_event: During a drought a man interrupted the Friday sermon to say that livestock were dying and the roads cut off, and asked the Prophet to pray for rain; rain then fell for a week until people returned asking him to pray for it to stop, and he said, in effect, around us and not upon us — whereupon the clouds broke apart over Medina.
islam.explanation: This well-known hadith of the istisqā (rain-seeking prayer) records a community harmed first by too little rain and then by too much within a single week.
islam.tie_back: It is a lived instance of the Kural's paradox: rain ruins and rain restores, and the difference is only measure and timing.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1013–1014 (Book of Istisqā), narrated by Anas ibn Malik
islam._accuracy_note: A strong narrative match on rain's two faces; summarised rather than quoted, since the hadith runs several paragraphs across two reports.

judaism.quote_or_event: Honi the Circle-Drawer, asked to pray for rain in a drought, drew a circle and refused to leave it until rain fell. Drops came, and he objected that he had asked for more; a violent, destructive downpour followed, and he objected again; only then did rain of goodwill and blessing fall.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah preserves this story as a study in the difference between rain that is too little, rain that is ruinous, and rain that is a blessing.
judaism.tie_back: It stages the Kural's whole couplet as a narrative — the same rain destroying and then lifting up.
judaism._accuracy_note: An unusually precise parallel on rain's destructive and restorative faces; paraphrased because the account is a multi-paragraph narrative.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Just as rain seeps into a poorly roofed house, lust seeps into an undeveloped mind. Just as rain doesn't seep into a well roofed house, lust doesn't seep into a well developed mind."
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pairs two verses in which the identical rain either penetrates and damages or is harmlessly shed, depending entirely on the condition of what receives it.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's structure of one rain producing opposite outcomes, though here the rain is harmful in both halves.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honest stretch: the antithetical structure and rain imagery match, but rain here is purely a simile for defilement, not a life-giving force that also restores.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Angered by human wickedness, Zeus unleashes unending rain and floods the world, drowning the whole race except Deucalion and Pyrrha; when the waters recede the pair are told to throw the bones of their mother behind them, and the stones they cast become a new human race.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's telling makes the same downpour the instrument of annihilation and the prelude to humanity's re-founding.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's couplet in mythic form: rain destroys utterly, and then the destroyed are raised up again.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.253–415 (the flood of Deucalion and Pyrrha)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on rain as both destroyer and precondition of renewal; the restoration comes from stones rather than from rain itself.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Philosophy, speaking in the voice of Fortune, tells Boethius that turning her wheel is simply what she is: she delights in raising the lowest to the top and bringing the highest down, and no one who steps onto the wheel may complain when it comes round.
philosophy.explanation: The Consolation uses the wheel to argue that a single impersonal power is responsible for both elevation and ruin, and that expecting only its upward motion is a category error.
philosophy.tie_back: It matches the Kural's insistence that one and the same force is the destroyer and the lifter-up — "all of it."
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose 2 (Fortune's wheel)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased rather than quoted because English translations of the wheel passage differ significantly; the parallel is structural, and Fortune is capricious where rain is not.

kurals.tamil:
விசும்பின் துளிவீழின் அல்லால்மற் றாங்கே
பசும்புல் தலைகாண்பு அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Visumbin thulivizhin allaal matraange,
Pasumpul thalaikaanbu aridhu.
kurals.meaning: Unless drops fall from the open sky, it will be hard to catch sight of even the tip of a single blade of green grass on the earth.
kurals.elementary: Put a seed in a pot of soil and give it no water at all. Nothing happens — not even a tiny green shoot. This kural says that is what the whole world would look like without rain: not one blade of grass anywhere.
kurals.university: விசும்பு (visumbu) is the open expanse of sky rather than the cloud, so the drop is imagined falling from the whole heavens at once. The argument is a fortiori and depends on Tamil biological classification: பசும்புல் (pasumpul), green grass, is the standard example of an ஓரறிவு உயிர் — a one-sense living being, the humblest grade of life in the Tamil-Jain scheme — so if even that cannot appear, nothing above it can. தலை here means the tip or head of the blade, sharpening the claim from "no grass" to "not even the tip of grass." The verse's spare, almost photographic minimalism has made it one of the most quoted lines of the chapter in Tamil environmental writing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "Forth burst the winds, down come the lightning-flashes: the plants shoot up, the realm of light is streaming. Food springs abundant for all living creatures, what time Parjanya quickens earth with moisture."
hinduism.explanation: The Rigveda's hymn to Parjanya, god of the rain-cloud, describes plants springing up the moment the storm breaks and moisture reaches the soil.
hinduism.tie_back: It states the positive form of the Kural's negative claim: the sprouting of plants begins exactly when the drops fall.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on rain as the sole trigger of vegetation; framed as praise of a deity rather than as the Kural's bare observation.

christianity.quote_or_event: "And every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground."
christianity.explanation: Genesis explains the pre-vegetative state of the newly made world by a single fact: it had not yet rained.
christianity.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's proposition — no drops from above, therefore no green thing below.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-identical logic, down to the emphasis on 'every herb of the field'; the only gap is Genesis's added mention of human tillage.

islam.quote_or_event: "And you see the earth barren, but when We send down upon it rain, it quivers and swells and grows [something] of every beautiful kind."
islam.explanation: The Qur'an contrasts the visibly dead, barren ground with the same ground stirring into growth the moment rain reaches it.
islam.tie_back: Both verses make the visible presence or absence of green growth the direct index of whether rain has fallen.
islam._accuracy_note: Extremely close on barren-ground-until-rain; the Qur'an dwells on the growth, the Kural on the barrenness.

judaism.quote_or_event: "There is not a single blade of grass that does not have a constellation in the firmament that strikes it and says to it: 'Grow.'"
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's midrash makes the growth of every individual blade of grass depend on a specific influence descending from the heavens.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural it insists that even the humblest blade of grass is entirely dependent on something coming down from the sky.
judaism._accuracy_note: The blade-of-grass-and-sky image is a remarkably close echo; English renderings vary (some read 'angel' for 'constellation'), and the celestial influence is astral rather than rainfall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "cows graze on the lush meadow grass … Right then a vast cloud rained forth, soaking the uplands and valleys."
buddhism.explanation: In the Dhaniya Sutta a wealthy cattleman and the Buddha trade verses each ending "so rain forth, heavens, if you wish," and at the close a great cloud does exactly that, soaking the grazing land the herdsman depends on.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's chain of rain to green pasture, though the sutta's real interest is in what makes a person ready for the rain.
buddhism.source: Dhaniya Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.2 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honest stretch: rain and grazing grass both appear, but the sutta never claims that without rain no grass grows.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "a most dreadful and cruel year for mankind over the all-nourishing earth: the ground would not make the seed sprout, for rich-crowned Demeter kept it hid"
greek_mythology.explanation: Grieving for Persephone, Demeter suspends the earth's fertility entirely, so that sown seed simply does not come up.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's image of an earth on which not even a green shoot can be seen.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, lines 305–309 (Evelyn-White translation)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on total failure of vegetation; the withheld agent is the goddess's blessing on seed rather than rainfall specifically.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "Lo, the rains perish which Ether-father throws / Down to the bosom of Earth-mother; but then / Upsprings the shining grain, and boughs are green / Amid the trees, and trees themselves wax big / And lade themselves with fruits"
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius uses rainfall to demonstrate his atomist thesis that nothing is annihilated: the rain vanishes, but reappears transformed as crops and foliage.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the Kural's claim a physical mechanism — the green blade is literally the rain in another form.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.250–254 (W. E. Leonard translation, 1916)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on rain as the direct material cause of green growth; Lucretius argues conservation of matter rather than dependence.

kurals.tamil:
நெடுங்கடலும் தன்நீர்மை குன்றும் தடிந்தெழிலி
தான்நல்கா தாகி விடின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nedungadalum than neermai kundrum thadinthezhili,
Thaan nalkaadhaagi vidin.
kurals.meaning: Even the long, vast sea will diminish in its own fullness if the cloud that has drawn its water up stops giving that water back.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a piggy bank you keep taking coins out of but never put any coins back into. Sooner or later it is empty. This kural says even the huge ocean is like that piggy bank: the clouds take water from it, and if they never return it as rain, even the sea runs low.
kurals.university: எழிலி (ezhili) is the rain-cloud and தடிந்து means "having cut off, drawn up," so the line describes evaporation as an act of extraction from the sea. The phrase தன் நீர்மை (than neermai) is a fine pun: நீர்மை means both "wateriness, fullness of water" and "one's own proper nature or quality," so the sea loses its water and its character at once. What makes the couplet remarkable is that it states a closed evaporation-and-precipitation cycle — cloud takes from ocean, must return to ocean — many centuries before that cycle was formalised in European science. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward also read a social allegory here, developed vigorously by Kalaignar Karunanidhi: those who rise out of a community and do not give back diminish the very source that raised them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "Uniform, with the passing days, this water mounts and fails again. The tempest-clouds give life to earth, and fires re-animate the heaven."
hinduism.explanation: This riddle-verse from the Rigveda's great cosmological hymn describes water as a single quantity that rises and descends in an unbroken rhythm.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe rain as the return leg of a circuit rather than a one-way gift.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on the up-and-down water cycle; the Rigveda does not add the Kural's specific point about the sea shrinking if the return fails.

christianity.quote_or_event: "For he maketh small the drops of water: they pour down rain according to the vapour thereof: which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly."
christianity.explanation: Elihu describes rain as vapour drawn up and then condensed back into drops — an explicit two-stage account of the water cycle.
christianity.tie_back: It supplies the mechanism the Kural relies on: the cloud must give back what it first drew up.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on the vapour-to-rain circuit; Job celebrates the giving and never contemplates the failure case that is the Kural's point.

islam.quote_or_event: "And We have sent down rain from the sky in a measured amount and settled it in the earth. And indeed, We are Able to take it away."
islam.explanation: The verse presents rainfall as a measured quantity deposited in the earth, with the explicit reminder that the same power can withdraw it.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's accounting sense of water as a finite stock that can be drawn down as well as replenished.
islam._accuracy_note: Genuine on water as measured and withdrawable, but the sea is not in view and the cycle is theological rather than physical.

judaism.quote_or_event: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes the circulation of water between sea and river as his opening example of nature's endless, unaccumulating repetition.
judaism.tie_back: It describes the same closed circuit the Kural describes, viewed from the rivers' side rather than the cloud's.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on the sea-and-return cycle; Kohelet draws a lesson about futility where the Kural draws one about reciprocity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Mendicants, when the ocean surges it makes the rivers surge. When the rivers surge they make the streams surge. When the streams surge they make the lakes surge … When the ocean recedes it makes the rivers recede."
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the linked rise and fall of ocean, rivers, streams and ponds as an image for how the twelve links of dependent origination swell and subside together.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's picture of ocean and the waters above it as one interdependent system that rises or falls as a whole.
buddhism.source: Upayanti Sutta, Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.69 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honest stretch: the ocean-and-waters interdependence is real, but it functions purely as a simile for dependent origination and involves no rain.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "deep-flowing Ocean, from whom all rivers flow and every sea, and all the springs and deep wells"
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles names Okeanos as the single ultimate reservoir from which every river, sea, spring and well derives its water.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts make the ocean the master account from which all other water is drawn, which is why its depletion would matter.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good on ocean as source of all waters; Homer sees only the outward flow and never the cloud's return, which is the Kural's real subject.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "When the sun is near, the stream of vapour flows upwards; when it recedes, the stream of water flows down, and the order of sequence, at all events, in this process always remains the same."
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sets out the first systematic Greek account of the hydrological cycle: solar heat lifts water as vapour, which cools and falls again, endlessly.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the scientific statement of the circuit the Kural assumes when it warns that the cloud must give back what it took.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Meteorologica II.2 / I.9, 346b (E. W. Webster translation)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent match on the closed evaporation-precipitation cycle; Aristotle is descriptive where Valluvar draws a consequence from it.

kurals.tamil:
சிறப்பொடு பூசனை செல்லாது வானம்
வறக்குமேல் வானோர்க்கும் ஈண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirappodu poosanai sellaadhu vaanam,
Varakkumel vaanorkkum eendu.
kurals.meaning: If the sky dries up, then here on earth neither the great festivals nor the daily worship offered to the celestials can go on at all.
kurals.elementary: You cannot have a birthday party if there is no food, no cake and no candles — the party just does not happen. This kural says the same about temple festivals and daily prayers: if the rain stops, there is nothing left to offer, and the celebrating stops too.
kurals.university: பூசனை (poosanai), from Sanskrit पूजा, denotes the regular daily offering, while சிறப்பு (sirappu) here carries its technical sense of the annual festival or special honour, so the couplet covers the whole ritual calendar from daily to yearly. வானோர் (vaanor), "those of the sky," is a neat counterpoint to வானம், the sky itself — the sky-dwellers are made hostage to the sky's own generosity. The adverb ஈண்டு ("here," i.e. in this world) localises the collapse: heaven is not harmed, but heaven's honours on earth cease. The argument is quietly subversive of ritual priority, inverting the ordinary Vedic sequence in which sacrifice causes rain, and it is one of the passages most often cited to show Valluvar's materially grounded, non-sectarian ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: "An oblation duly thrown into the fire, reaches the sun; from the sun comes rain, from rain food, therefrom the living creatures (derive their subsistence)."
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes a closed circuit in which ritual offering generates rain, rain generates food, and food generates the creatures who will make the next offering.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural cuts the same circuit at a different point: break the rain link and the offering at the other end becomes impossible.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong on the ritual-rain-food loop; Manu runs the causation from sacrifice to rain, while Valluvar pointedly runs it the other way.

christianity.quote_or_event: "The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the LORD; the priests, the LORD'S ministers, mourn."
christianity.explanation: Joel's account of a devastating agricultural catastrophe notes that the Temple's grain and wine offerings simply stop, because there is no grain and no wine to offer.
christianity.tie_back: It is exactly the Kural's claim: when the land dries up, worship itself cannot proceed.
christianity._accuracy_note: An almost exact parallel — drought halting both daily offering and priestly ritual — from a text Valluvar could not have known.

islam.quote_or_event: "And if only the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied [the messengers], so We seized them for what they were earning."
islam.explanation: The Qur'an links a community's religious state to whether the heavens open over it with blessing.
islam.tie_back: It binds worship and rainfall together as the Kural does, but reverses the direction of dependence — here piety conditions rain rather than rain conditioning piety.
islam._accuracy_note: Honest partial match: the rain-and-worship pairing is genuine, but the causal arrow runs opposite to the Kural's, which is the whole point of Valluvar's verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: "At four times of the year the world is judged: On Passover judgment is passed concerning grain; on Shavuot concerning fruits that grow on a tree … and on the festival of Sukkot they are judged concerning water, i.e., the rainfall of the coming year."
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah organises the entire pilgrimage-festival calendar around agricultural verdicts, with the autumn festival of Sukkot devoted to the coming year's rain — the occasion of the Temple's water-libation ceremony.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts make festivals and rainfall a single interlocked system rather than separate spheres.
judaism.source: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:2 (Koren–Steinsaltz, William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on festival life being structured around rain; the Mishnah has festivals petitioning for rain, not ceasing for lack of it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Vinaya establishes the vassa, the three-month rains retreat: monks must settle in one place for the monsoon rather than wander, and the year's central communal observances — including the Kathina robe ceremony that follows it — are timed entirely by the rainy season.
buddhism.explanation: The monastic ritual calendar of Theravada Buddhism is literally built around the arrival and departure of the monsoon rains.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural it treats the rhythm of religious observance as something set by the rain rather than independent of it.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Piṭaka, Mahāvagga III (Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka, the chapter on entering the rains)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Real and structural link between rain and ritual life, but the vassa is organised by rain's presence, not disrupted by its absence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "So she would have destroyed the whole race of men with cruel famine and have robbed them who dwell on Olympus of their glorious right of gifts and sacrifices, had not Zeus perceived and marked this in his heart."
greek_mythology.explanation: Demeter's withdrawal of the earth's fertility threatens not only humanity but the Olympians themselves, who would lose the offerings that only a fed humanity can make.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact argument: when the earth stops yielding, the gods are the ones deprived of their worship.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, lines 310–313 (Evelyn-White translation)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: One of the closest cross-cultural matches in the chapter — celestials losing their sacrifices because the earth has stopped producing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero's Stoic speaker explains that whenever something brought great benefit to humankind, the ancients took it to come from divine goodness and gave the thing itself the name of a god — so that grain came to be called Ceres and wine Liber.
philosophy.explanation: The argument makes the names and cults of certain gods derivative of the material goods they supply.
philosophy.tie_back: It runs parallel to the Kural's inversion: the honours paid to the celestials depend on the material bounty that makes those honours possible.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased because English renderings of the passage differ; the parallel is about worship being grounded in material benefit, not about drought halting ritual.

kurals.tamil:
தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா வியன்உலகம்
வானம் வழங்கா தெனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaanam thavam irandum thangaa viyan ulagam,
Vaanam vazhangaadhenin.
kurals.meaning: If the sky stops giving its rain, then neither charity toward others nor austerity practised on one's own account can survive anywhere in this wide world.
kurals.elementary: You cannot share your lunch with a friend if you have no lunch, and it is not brave to skip a meal if there was never any food to skip. This kural says that giving to others and going without on purpose both need there to be something in the world first — and rain is what puts it there.
kurals.university: The two nouns are the twin pillars of Valluvar's ethical architecture: தானம் (thaanam, Sanskrit dāna) is the householder's virtue of giving, treated at length in chapter 23 ஈகை, while தவம் (thavam, Sanskrit tapas) is the renunciant's discipline, treated in chapter 27. By yoking them in a single line and making both contingent on rainfall, Valluvar establishes the material precondition of the entire இல்லறவியல் and துறவறவியல் sections before he has begun to expound either. The verb தங்கா ("will not abide, will not stay") is carefully chosen — it is not that such acts become wrong, but that they can no longer hold their place in the world. The move is characteristic: ethics in the Kural is never floated free of the economy that supports it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Upanishad, gods, humans and demons each come to Prajapati for instruction and each receives the single syllable "Da," from the voice of the thunder. Each hears it differently: the gods hear damyata, restrain yourselves; humans hear datta, give; demons hear dayadhvam, be compassionate.
hinduism.explanation: The thunder of the rain-cloud is made the teacher of the three great disciplines, with self-restraint and giving at the head of the list.
hinduism.tie_back: The Upanishad has the rain-cloud itself pronouncing the very two virtues — giving and self-restraint — that this Kural makes depend on rain.
hinduism.source: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2.1–3 (the teaching of the thunder, 'Da Da Da')
hinduism._accuracy_note: A striking convergence — thunder teaching dāna and dama — though the Upanishad makes rain the teacher of the virtues, not their material precondition; paraphrased because translations of the syllables differ.

christianity.quote_or_event: "Now he that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness;"
christianity.explanation: Paul, urging the Corinthians to a collection for the poor, argues that God's supply of seed and bread is what makes generous giving possible and fruitful.
christianity.tie_back: It makes the same link the Kural makes — material provision from above is the precondition of charitable giving.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on provision grounding generosity; Paul's confidence that the supply will come differs from the Kural's warning about its failure.

islam.quote_or_event: "And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking means to the approval of Allah and assuring [reward for] themselves is like a garden on high ground which is hit by a downpour - so it yields its fruits in double."
islam.explanation: The Qur'an likens sincere charitable spending to a well-sited garden struck by heavy rain, which returns twice the harvest.
islam.tie_back: Charity is figured precisely as a rain-fed yield, matching the Kural's claim that giving depends on what the sky supplies.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on rain as the image and enabler of charity; the verse uses rain as simile for reward rather than as literal precondition.

judaism.quote_or_event: "Where there is no bread, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no bread."
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah states the mutual dependence of material sustenance and religious life — study and observance cannot be sustained by a starving community.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's proposition in rabbinic form: spiritual practice cannot abide in the world without the food that underwrites it.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (Mishnah Yomit, Dr. Joshua Kulp translation)
judaism._accuracy_note: Exceptionally close on material provision as the precondition of religious life; the Jewish text does not name rain, and adds a reciprocal dependence the Kural does not.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "As water raining on a hill / flows down to the valley, / even so does what is given here / benefit the dead."
buddhism.explanation: This verse on offerings made for departed relatives uses rainwater running downhill as the image of how a gift made here reaches those who can no longer provide for themselves.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts join rain and dāna directly, treating giving as something that flows from an upstream supply.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Genuine pairing of rain imagery with generosity, but rain here is a simile for how merit travels, not the condition that makes giving possible.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus and Hermes travel in Phrygia disguised as poor strangers and are turned away from a thousand homes; only the elderly Baucis and Philemon share their meagre supper. The gods then flood the whole ungenerous district, spare the old couple's cottage, and transform it into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's tale ties together hospitality, divine water sent in judgement, and the founding of a place of worship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It brings giving, rain and piety into one story, though it does not make giving depend on rainfall as the Kural does.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak next-best match: the elements of generosity, water from the sky and worship all appear, but the causal claim of the Kural is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "it is impossible, or not easy, to do noble acts without the proper equipment"
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtuous activity requires external goods — friends, wealth, political power — as its instruments, so material circumstance conditions how far a life can be excellent.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the general philosophical form of the Kural's specific claim that charity and austerity cannot abide without the rain that supplies them.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on virtue requiring material means; Aristotle speaks of wealth and friends generally, not of the natural supply that generates them.

kurals.tamil:
நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகெனின் யார்யார்க்கும்
வான்இன்று அமையாது ஒழுக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Neer indru amaiyaadhu ulagenin yaaryaarkkum,
Vaan indru amaiyaadhu ozhukku.
kurals.meaning: If it is true that the world cannot carry on for anyone at all without water, then it is just as true that right conduct cannot carry on without rain.
kurals.elementary: Think of electricity in a house. The lights, the fridge, the heating — none of it works if the power is cut. This kural says rain is the power supply for the whole world, and even being good to each other gets much harder when it fails.
kurals.university: The couplet's force rests on a deliberate pun in its final word, ஒழுக்கு (ozhukku), which means both "a flowing, a stream" and, through its near-twin ஒழுக்கம், "right conduct" — the subject of chapter 14. Valluvar thereby makes one word carry both the hydrological and the moral sense of "keeping to its proper course," closing the chapter by fusing the two. யார்யார்க்கும் ("for anyone whosoever") universalises the claim across rank, region and creed, an emphasis that recurs throughout the Kural's ethics. Placed as the last verse of the chapter, it is the hinge that carries the reader into chapters 3 and 4 on the greatness of the renunciant and the assertion of virtue: the whole moral edifice that follows has just been shown to rest on rainfall.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita sets out a turning wheel in which prescribed duty produces sacrifice, sacrifice produces rain, rain produces food, and food produces living beings; Krishna then says that whoever does not help turn this wheel lives in vain.
hinduism.explanation: Rain is a load-bearing link in a single circuit that runs from moral obligation through nature and back to moral obligation again.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes right conduct and rainfall parts of one system rather than separate domains.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14–16 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match linking duty and rain in one cycle; summarised across three verses, and the Gita's arrow runs from duty to rain rather than rain to conduct.

christianity.quote_or_event: "For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God:"
christianity.explanation: Hebrews uses rain-fed ground yielding a useful crop as the image of a human life that responds rightly to what it has received.
christianity.tie_back: It makes the same move as the Kural's pun, letting rain-fed fruitfulness stand simultaneously for agricultural and moral productivity.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on rain-and-moral-fruitfulness held together; Hebrews uses the rain figuratively, where the Kural also means it literally.

islam.quote_or_event: "And said, 'Ask forgiveness of your Lord. Indeed, He is ever a Perpetual Forgiver. He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in [continuing] showers.'"
islam.explanation: Noah tells his people that setting their moral account right with God is what will open the sky over them in abundant rain.
islam.tie_back: Both verses tie rainfall and right conduct into a single proposition, refusing to treat them as unrelated.
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong on the rain-and-conduct linkage; the dependence runs from conduct to rain, the inverse of Valluvar's direction.

judaism.quote_or_event: "That I will give you the rain of your land in his due season, the first rain and the latter rain, that thou mayest gather in thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil … And then the LORD'S wrath be kindled against you, and he shut up the heaven, that there be no rain"
judaism.explanation: The second paragraph of the Shema, recited twice daily, makes the rainfall of the land the direct consequence of Israel's faithfulness or unfaithfulness.
judaism.tie_back: It is the most systematic statement anywhere of the Kural's thesis that rain and right conduct stand or fall together.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 11:13–17 (KJV, rendering the Hebrew Tanakh; the second paragraph of the Shema)
judaism._accuracy_note: Outstanding thematic match on rain bound to conduct; the causation is theological and runs conduct-to-rain, while the Kural runs rain-to-conduct.

buddhism.quote_or_event: "Furthermore, humans become unprincipled. This is the fifth obstacle to rain, which the forecasters don't know, and which their vision does not traverse."
buddhism.explanation: Listing five causes of drought that no weather-reader can detect, the Buddha ends with human beings becoming adhammika — unrighteous, not living by Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: It makes rainfall and moral conduct two faces of one order, exactly as the Kural's closing pun does.
buddhism.source: Vassa Sutta (Obstacles to Rain), Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.197 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong and unusually explicit pairing of unrighteousness with failed rain; the dependence again runs conduct-to-rain rather than rain-to-conduct.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: "Neither famine nor disaster ever haunt men who do true justice; but light-heartedly they tend the fields which are all their care. The earth bears them victual in plenty, and on the mountains the oak bears acorns upon the top and bees in the midst."
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's just city is rewarded with fertility and plenty, while the unjust city is visited with famine — justice and harvest are one subject for him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's closing line, it refuses to separate the moral order of a community from the productivity of its land.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the fusion of justice and agricultural plenty; Hesiod again makes conduct the cause and harvest the effect.

philosophy.quote_or_event: "It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness."
philosophy.explanation: Marx's 1859 formulation of historical materialism holds that the material conditions of production shape the ideas, morality and institutions a society is able to sustain.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the modern, secular form of the Kural's final claim: the moral life of a people rests on the material base that supports it.
philosophy.source: Karl Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on material conditions grounding morality, and it runs in the Kural's direction; Marx's base is the mode of production rather than rainfall.
